title: 2026 Mid-Year Fiscal Policy Review of the Government of Ghana for the 2026 Financial Year (Resetting for Growth, Jobs, and Economic Transformation)
presented_by: Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson (MP), Minister for Finance, on the authority of President John Dramani Mahama
headline_summary: No supplementary estimate was sought: the 2026 appropriation (GH¢357.1bn), total revenue and grants (GH¢268.1bn) and total expenditure (GH¢302.5bn) are unchanged, and the macro targets (GDP growth of at least 4.8%, inflation 8±2%, primary surplus 1.5% of GDP, reserves of at least 3 months of imports) are reaffirmed. Within the envelope, GH¢5.0bn is reallocated to the Ghana Gold Board to fund the cost of the Ghana Accelerated National Reserve Accumulation Policy (GANRAP), financed by cutting foreign-financed capex by GH¢3.0bn (slow bilateral loan disbursements) and GoG Big Push capex by GH¢2.0bn. First-half outturns beat programme: Q1 GDP growth 6.4%, June inflation 5.3%, primary surplus 0.9% of GDP vs a programmed deficit of 0.2%, debt 45.0% of GDP; expenditure ran GH¢31.3bn below programme, while oil revenue (GH¢6.3bn vs GH¢9.1bn) and arrears clearance (GH¢5.3bn vs GH¢14.0bn) fell short. The review also announces a post-ECF IMF Policy Coordination Instrument and a plan to cut the primary-surplus rule from 1.5% to 0.5% of GDP from 2027, and lays Customs and Excise Bills before Parliament.

new_measures.measure: GANRAP funding: GH¢5.0bn allocated to the Ghana Gold Board for reserve accumulation costs; annual allocations to continue until targets are met
Customs Bill: statutory maximum warehousing periods (perishables 3 months, general goods 6, raw materials 12) and re-warehousing capped at 6 months, with e-inventory systems linked to Customs
First Port Duty Rule: duties and taxes on transit goods become due at the first port of entry
Free Zones tightening: new licences only for genuine manufacturers, raw materials to be used within 12 months, exemptions limited to eligible raw materials
Mandatory Tax Identification Number for importers, statutory timelines for declarations, and improved valuation of leasehold transactions
Enforce bank guarantees on lifting refined petroleum products; movements only via approved pipelines and tracked systems
Remove the tax exemption on bunkering services
Excise Duty Bill: hybrid (ad valorem + specific) excise on wines and spirits
Review of sliding-scale excise rates on beer and stout
Excise compliance: e-registration of stockists, nationwide track-and-trace, penalties up to 3x the duty for tampering, bank guarantees
Abolish the 20% excise duty on locally manufactured fruit juices (introduced in 2023)
Nationwide rollout of a cross-border VAT collection system for non-resident digital platforms (piloted April 2026); projected GH¢2.3bn in the first full year
Fiscal Electronic Devices rollout with a VAT Reward Scheme for customers who obtain valid VAT invoices
Publican AI vehicle-valuation module to be rolled out next
Block new Import Declaration Forms while earlier ones are unretired; retirement limited to 90 days (general goods) and 120 days (equipment and capital goods)
Ghana Card number to be the sole Tax Identification Number for all tax transactions

Public Procurement Act reforms: limit single-source and restricted tendering, sanctions for breaches, shorter lead times (national goods tendering 23 to 8 weeks; international works tendering 27 to 14 weeks)
Fiscal rule change: primary-surplus floor cut from 1.5% to 0.5% of GDP from 2027, with the space reserved for growth-enhancing capex; PFM amendment to come with the 2027 Budget
36-month IMF Policy Coordination Instrument (non-financing) with 26 reform targets running to end-2027
Amend the PFM Act's Sinking Fund provisions and issue Sinking Fund Regulations; 7% of non-oil tax revenue plus domestic bond proceeds pledged to the Sinking Fund
Emergency flood response: GH¢350m to the Disaster Management Committee and GH¢226m to MWHWR flood mitigation; a permanent flood solution to be funded in the 2027 Budget
Acquisition of high-occupancy buses for Metro Mass Transit and STC
BoG recapitalisation bond issued in March 2026, with annual provisions until BoG equity is restored

commitment_progress.evidence: Real GDP grew 6.4% in Q1 2026 against the 'at least 4.8%' full-year target; the target is reaffirmed.
Non-oil GDP grew 6.3% in Q1 2026 against the 'at least 4.9%' target.
Inflation was 5.3% in June 2026 (3.2% in March), below the 8±2% year-end band.
The H1 commitment-basis primary surplus was 0.9% of GDP (GH¢14,678.7m) against a programmed deficit of 0.2%; the 1.5% target is unchanged.
The H1 overall deficit was 0.4% of GDP (commitment) vs a 2.0% target, and 0.8% (cash) vs 2.9%; the full-year 2.2%/4.0% targets are retained.
Gross reserves were US$12.9bn at end-June 2026, or 5.0 months of imports, against the minimum of 3 months.
H1 total revenue and grants were GH¢124.8bn vs a programme of GH¢126.1bn (7.8% vs 7.9% of GDP); the GH¢268.1bn full-year projection is preserved.
H1 net non-oil tax revenue was GH¢99,918.8m vs a programme of GH¢100,052.8m (6.4% vs 6.5% of GDP); the full-year GH¢216.1bn is unchanged.
H1 non-oil domestic revenue was 7.4% of GDP vs a programme of 7.3%; the 15.7% full-year figure is unchanged in Appendix 3B.

Act 1151 abolished the COVID-19 levy, cut the effective VAT rate from 21.9% to 20% and raised the registration threshold from GH¢200,000 to GH¢750,000. Residual COVID levy receipts were GH¢324.9m in H1 (p.99).
Customs and Excise Bills were laid before Parliament with the mid-year review (early). The income tax law review is a PCI target for end-June 2027 (p.68), after the 2027 Budget.
Total expenditure is kept at GH¢302.5bn in the revision. H1 spending was GH¢127.2bn vs a programme of GH¢158.6bn.
H1 arrears clearance was GH¢5.3bn vs a programme of GH¢14.0bn, with no IPP legacy arrears cleared (programme GH¢2.5bn). No new arrears accumulated.
Government has paid US$497.7m, about 42% of the agreed IPP legacy debt, more than the US$345m committed. Renegotiated PPAs were approved in February 2026 (US$250m immediate savings).

A Transaction Adviser for ECG/NEDCo private participation was appointed in June 2026. The implementation strategy is due by end-2026 (PCI: Cabinet approval end-December 2026), so a Q3 2026 award looks unlikely.
No update on restoring World Bank-backed standby letters of credit.

The 1,200MW plant at Kafodzidzi-Abrobeano has confirmed feasibility, permitting under way and GE Vernova turbines secured (35-45% savings). Start of construction is not reported; the first 600MW is due in 2028.
Four local contractors are extending electricity in the Oti, Volta, Central and Savannah Regions, with completion expected within six months; 343 more communities are to be connected by end-2026.
GNPC Explorco 'remains on course' to start exploratory drilling in the Voltaian Basin in Q4 2026.
AKSA Anwomaso's first 171MW phase was commissioned and synchronised (200MW by year-end). The 100MW Cenit plant is about 90% complete.
Work has started on 87 Big Push projects; 13 are at 50%+ and 6 above 75%. GH¢6.5bn was paid to the programme (p.91), but GoG Big Push capex was cut by GH¢2.0bn in the revision (p.106).
No update on the 10km-per-constituency roads programme.
By end-June 2026, routine maintenance covered 462km of trunk roads, 6,122km of feeder roads and 4,760km of urban roads (11,344km in total).
Implementation has begun: US$523m to rehabilitate 1,050km of feeder roads in four agricultural clusters across 13 regions.
No update on the Tema-Mpakadan railway or the Accra-Kumasi Eastern Line.
Establishment of 50 Farmer Service Centres has started. GH¢551m is in a BoG escrow account for a letter of credit for 1,840 machines, fewer than the 4,000+ planned.
Only 300mt each of maize and Agyapa rice seed and 18,684mt of inorganic fertiliser (plus 96,000 litres of organic) were procured, against targets of 4,388mt, 31,000mt and 272,000mt.
Oil palm land bank: 270,000ha reviewed in the Western Region and 10,780ha found suitable; about 30,000ha is expected for phase one, and the bank could exceed 100,000ha.
No update on the seven agro-processing plants; only transaction-adviser work on Komenda Sugar, Northern Star Tomato and other dormant firms is reported (p.83).
A Transaction Adviser has been engaged for the three garment factories (Bono East, Central, Eastern), expected to create about 27,000 direct jobs.
No update on MSME access to AfCFTA markets.
A US$300m World Bank-financed project (210 interventions) will support ending double-track. Completion of the single-track transition is not reported.
The World Bank project includes upgrading 30 Category C schools to B and 20 Category B to A (the budget said 10), plus 10 new SHSs. E-Blocks are not mentioned.
No update on the 200 JHS, primary and KG schools, bungalows or toilets.
No update on mono-desks, buses or pick-ups for schools.
GH¢915m has been paid for Ministry of Education goods and services 'including sanitary pads and the Capitation Grant'. Extension to all SHSs is not explicitly confirmed.
No update on the University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences, Bunso.
No update on new regional hospitals or the Bole and Shama district hospitals.
No update on completing abandoned Agenda 111 hospitals.
No update on the seven maternal and child health hospital upgrades.

The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (MahamaCares) received GH¢1.1bn (p.90), started three cardiology centres and enrolled 168 patients for specialised treatment support. A formal NCD financing policy is not reported.
No update on the Damongo, Tamale, Yendi or Bawku water systems.
No update on household or public toilets.
No update on Saglemi housing or Rent-to-Own.
No update on the new cell sites.
No update on Girls-in-ICT. The One Million Coders Programme has 140,000 registrants and 40,000 enrolled (p.85).

The 100th LEAP payment cycle reached about 1.5m individuals, and 226,930 households graduated. New households are still being validated, and the PCI now targets 470,000 households by end-December 2026 (p.67), so the March 2026 target is not confirmed as met.
No update on raising the DACF disability share to 5%. GH¢4.4bn was paid to the DACF (p.90).
No update on offshore patrol vessels, helicopters or aircraft.
No update on fire tenders.
No hectares of reclaimed land are reported, only a pledge to 'improve supervision of land reclamation' (p.83).
No update on stadia.
The review states 'We established the Fiscal Council' (p.15). Full operationalisation (secretariat head, staff, MoUs) is a PCI reform target (p.66).
The Value for Money Office has been established (p.15); full operationalisation is a PCI target for end-June 2027 (p.68). Mandatory VfM certificates are not mentioned.
NIB, ADB and CBG were recapitalised in 2025. UMB was fully recapitalised by GAT and Prudential Bank through a private-sector-led approach.
GSS has started GDP and CPI rebasing, with completion planned by June 2027. 'Ghana in Numbers' and the Tourism Satellite Account are not mentioned.
In April 2026 Ghana raised GH¢2.7bn through its first seven-year cedi bond since the 2022 default.
No banking NPL ratio is reported.
No aggregate job-creation figure for 2026 is reported.
No update on company registrations or EOCO recoveries.

shortfalls_admitted.text: Oil revenue was below target: upstream receipts GH¢6.3bn vs an H1 target of GH¢9.1bn.
Total revenue and grants were GH¢124.8bn vs a GH¢126.1bn target; non-oil non-tax revenue GH¢9.8bn vs GH¢11.0bn; domestic revenue 7.7% vs 7.8% of GDP.
One ECF quantitative performance criterion (the ceiling on BoG claims on government) was missed because of the accounting of the recapitalisation bond.
Foreign-financed capex cut by GH¢3.0bn because of slow bilateral loan disbursements.
Government could not use the GH¢350m Contingency Fund draw for flood relief because of a High Court garnishee order.
Ghana loses an estimated 60% of potential VAT revenue through non-compliance.
Publican AI does not yet cover vehicle valuation, the largest customs revenue component.
VAT Act 1151 regulations will not be developed until 2027.
GDP/CPI rebasing will not be finished until June 2027.
The Minister acknowledges that many households still face difficulties ('low inflation alone does not refill an empty pot').

risks: Middle East conflict: energy-price shock (Brent rose from US$66.6 to US$103.1 between January and March 2026) and higher food, fertiliser and transport costs (pp.22-23)
Global growth slowing to 3.0% in 2026 with tighter financial conditions and higher bond yields (p.22)
Cocoa price fell from US$5,018 to US$3,241 per tonne between January and March 2026 (p.24)
Large DDEP maturities: GH¢58bn in 2027 and GH¢53bn in 2028 (GH¢111bn), with GH¢30bn due in February 2027 (pp.41-42)
Recurring floods and climate risk; the permanent solution is deferred to the 2027 Budget (pp.10, 60)
Outstanding non-bonded commercial debt restructurings (ICBC US$255m, ATIDI) still pending OCC approval (p.40)
Rising services inflation (9.4%) and non-food inflation (6.3%) in June 2026 (p.30)
Cedi depreciated about 7.9% against the US$ in H1 2026 after the 2025 appreciation (p.45)
Lower primary-surplus floor (0.5% of GDP) from 2027 loosens the fiscal anchor (p.69)
Arrears-clearance and capex execution lagging (H1 capex GH¢22.2bn vs GH¢36.6bn programmed) (p.99)
data_quality_notes: Section 5 (p.62) reaffirms 'real GDP growth of at least 4.9%' and 'non-oil growth of at least 4.8%', swapping the budget figures (4.8% and 4.9%) restated on pp.11 and 26. The budget values are used.
June 2026 inflation is 5.3% on pp.26, 30 and 92 but 5.7% on p.18; 5.3% is used.
End-2024 debt/GDP appears as 61.8% (pp.18, 24) and 61.6% (p.36 and Figure 7).
2025 debt service as a share of domestic revenue is 28.8% on p.18 and 28.6% on p.37.
Figure 10 (p.45) shows -5.3% for one June-2026 currency, while the text gives -5.0% vs EUR. The text values (-7.9% USD, -6.5% GBP, -5.0% EUR) are used.

The text (p.35) reports H1 total expenditure on a cash basis of GH¢136.9bn vs GH¢172.5bn. Appendix 2A (p.99) gives commitment-basis expenditure of GH¢127,234.9m vs GH¢158,555.7m; 136.9 appears to equal expenditure plus arrears clearance plus the GH¢4,363.0m discrepancy.
H1 cash overall balance is -0.8% of GDP (GH¢-12,165.4m) including a GH¢-4,363.0m statistical discrepancy, or -0.5% (GH¢-7,802.4m) before it (p.99).

The conclusion's 'payments made so far' list (pp.90-91) differs from Appendix 2A H1 figures (e.g. compensation GH¢48.8bn vs GH¢42.9bn; capex GH¢11.5bn plus Big Push GH¢6.5bn vs GH¢22.2bn) and seems to cover a different period or definition.
Appendix 2A shows zero H1 clearance of IPP legacy arrears, while p.74 says US$497.7m of IPP legacy debt has been paid; the payment channel is not reconciled.
The GH¢2.0bn cut to GoG Big Push capex appears only in Appendix 3C (p.106); the text (p.63) mentions only the GH¢3.0bn foreign-financed capex cut and the GH¢5.0bn GANRAP allocation.
Appendix 3B (p.105) prints grants as 0.6% of GDP; GH¢3,066m is 0.2% of GDP (p.101 shows 0.2).

Appendix page titles are mislabelled (pp.96-98 are headed '2A', '3B' and '4C' for 2025 tables). Several tables (Table 3 and Appendices 2A-3C) are garbled in the text extraction and were re-read with PyMuPDF.
Revised end-2026 benchmark oil price and output are not given; the oil-revenue projection is unchanged.
Cenit plant is described as 100MW (p.83), against 300MW in the 2026 Budget commitment.
Monetary amounts in GH¢ million were converted from full-cedi appendix figures and rounded to one decimal place. Figures stated in billions in the text (e.g. debt stock) are multiplied by 1,000.
Page numbers are PDF page indices (printed page number + 9 for the main text).
